title: Why do pressure cookers cook food faster?

scenes.title: Why pressure cooks faster
scenes.narration: Ever noticed how rajma or chana can take hours in an ordinary pot, but much less time in a pressure cooker? The secret is not a special ingredient. It is the pressure changing the temperature of the water around the food.
scenes.visual_label: Rajma and chana soften faster when cooking temperature rises.

scenes.title: Steam gets trapped
scenes.narration: In an open pot, steam escapes as water boils, so liquid water stays near one hundred degrees Celsius at sea level. A pressure cooker traps steam. As more steam collects inside, pressure increases; the regulator lets excess steam escape and helps keep pressure controlled.
scenes.visual_label: Trapped steam raises pressure while a regulator releases excess.

scenes.title: Water gets hotter
scenes.narration: Higher pressure raises water’s boiling point. That means water and steam inside a properly working cooker can become hotter than water boiling in an open pot. The hotter liquid transfers heat to the rajma or chana more quickly, helping it soften sooner. Imagine a small thermometer beside each pot: the cooker can reach the higher temperature.
scenes.visual_label: Higher pressure raises boiling temperature and speeds heat transfer.

scenes.title: Pressure, heat, faster cooking
scenes.narration: The safety valve and vent matter because they control pressure and release excess steam. Keep them clear and follow the cooker’s instructions. The core idea is simple: trapped steam raises pressure, pressure lets water get hotter, and hotter water cooks food faster. That is why a pressure cooker can save time and fuel.
scenes.visual_label: Clear vent + working regulator = controlled pressure.
